uncited: *   **Input:** 3D Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients), camera parameters (view/projection matrices), image resolution, tile configuration (default 16×16 pixels).
*   **Gaussian Batch:** A contiguous array of Gaussian primitives.
Each Gaussian contains screen-space center $(u, v)$, covariance matrix elements (or eigenvalues/vectors), opacity $\alpha$, and color coefficients.
*   **Tile Data:** A 2D grid of tiles covering the image.
Each tile contains a list of assigned splats.
**Instancing:** The image is divided into tiles, and splats are duplicated into each tile they overlap.
During this stage, a coarse culling is performed: the splat’s maximum opacity is computed in each assigned tile.
*   **Tile Subdivision:** Each image tile (e.g., 16×16 pixels) is subdivided into sub-tiles.
*   **Geometric Culling:** For each sub-tile, the warp checks if any splats in the current batch have geometric overlap with the sub-tile's pixel region.
*   **Batch Processing:** Splat data is processed in batches of 256 splats.
On NVIDIA RTX 2070 Super, it is up to 32% faster.
Across all tested GPUs (RTX 4090, RTX 3090, RTX 2070 Super), the changes reduce frame time over Faster-GS by 17% (+20% FPS) on average (geometric mean).
*   **Complexity:** The baseline alpha-blending GPU kernel (Faster-GS) performs two to three times slower than the optimistic theoretical bound.
3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [Kerbl et al. 2023] has become a dominant technique for novel view synthesis.
Despite thousands of follow-up methods, there is still room for improvement in rendering speed.
